extracted.intended_audience: experimental natural philosophers / Royal Society members / practicing experimental scientists attempting to reproduce prism/colour experiments
extracted.subtask_description: Reproduce and evaluate 17th‑century prism/spectrum experiments (image length vs breadth, colour order) using controlled prism geometry, lighting, and careful measurement; assess whether demonstrations (experimentum crucis) prove different refrangibility of light. Targeted at experiment replication and critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prism angle controls image length
rubrics_metrics.description: The larger the angle of the prism, the greater will be the length in proportion to the breadth of the image; by taking an angle of 70 or 75 degrees (or a little greater) the length may be many times the breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prisms with sufficiently large refracting angle; recommended angles mentioned: the author's used about 63°12', other trials at 56°–74°; to make the image as long as asserted, use angle ~66–67° or larger, or up to 70–75° to obtain lengths 5–8 times the breadth. Report the prism angle exactly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prism face figure and refractive power matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The figure (flat/convex/concave) of the prism sides and the refractive power of the glass materially affect the image breadth and length and the definition of its sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer prisms whose sides are not hollow ground; plain sides or very slightly convex are better (convex gives better definition). Note refractive power differences between glasses — prisms made of glass with greater refractive power produce longer images for the same angle. Examine whether a prism's sides are hollow ground (concave) which will increase breadth proportionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prisms that refract enough to make length ≈ five times breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments (and the experimentum crucis) should be made with prisms which refract so much as to make the length of the image five times its breadth, and rather more than less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prism does not produce length ≈5× breadth, the critical experiments may not 'succeed so plainly'. Choose or craft prisms (angle + glass) to meet this condition before attempting the decisive demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure the utmost length (faintest red to faintest blue)
rubrics_metrics.description: The utmost length of the image — from the faintest red at one end to the faintest blue at the other — must be measured; do not count the glaring light that sometimes shoots beyond the colours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When measuring, exclude transient glaring lights beyond the colours; if measures are taken right, the whole length will exceed the length of the straight sides by about the breadth of the image. Always state exactly which portion was measured (utmost length).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report precise geometry and distances
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide exact measures for the length and breadth of the image and its distance from the prism, set down exactly in feet and inches, and parts of an inch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include: prism angle, breadth of the hole in the shutter, distance from prism to wall (e.g., examples used: distance 18 ft 4 in), breadth of image (examples: 1 inch, 1⅓ inch), and the sun's diameter as reference. Use accurate instruments (sector for angles) and give numeric tables of trials (angles vs. image length).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and report ambient illumination and weather conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambient light (white sky/cloudiness) affects the visible length of the colours: clearest days make colours visible to a greater length; cloudy/brighter sky shortens the visible image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform trials on clear days for maximum colour length; note cloud cover changes during the experiment as they can make the image grow longer or shorter. Record sky conditions and consider repeating on different days to confirm stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a decisive experiment (experimentum crucis) over many minor tests
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not number of experiments but weight to be regarded; a single demonstrative (crucial) experiment that proves different refrangibility of light suffices, and other trials should focus on examining that demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and prioritize an experimentum crucis to test the key proposition; if that demonstration is sound, secondary experiments are unnecessary for the central claim. If it fails, show the fault in the demonstration rather than multiplying peripheral tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for confounding variables and apparatus imperfections
rubrics_metrics.description: Various circumstances can cause differences between observers: prism side figure, refractive power of glass, exactness of angle measurement, placement of the prism, variations in the sun's diameter at different times of year, and small errors in measuring lines and angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify, quantify, and report possible sources of discrepancy. Advise correspondents to check prism flatness/convexity, verify angle measurements (use sector), and consider seasonal/astronomical variations. Suggest remedies (e.g., use an object-glass of a telescope to define the round solar image when prism removed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary neighbouring illumination and objects to test origin of colours
rubrics_metrics.description: Colours in the retinal/retained image are influenced by neighbouring light and objects; placing illuminated or less illuminated bodies behind or adjacent to the paper circle changes the colours' situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform controlled manipulations: place test circle near shutter vs in open air, add/cover nearby illuminated objects, or use coloured liquids/filters to probe transparency and transmission (examples given: paper circle, two coloured liquids stacked). Record effects to distinguish intrinsic refrangibility from extrinsic/contingent influences.
